name: Cefazolin
high_alert_note: Not confirmed as high-alert on a source read; the institution's list governs.
summary: Cephalosporin antibacterial for infections caused by susceptible organisms (the product read is cefazolin in dextrose). Nursing focus: hypersensitivity with penicillin allergy, diarrhoea and prothrombin activity.
evidence_type_note: The evidence here is a regulator product label (prescribing information written for prescribers and pharmacists). It is not a bedside nursing practice guideline: the nursing actions are inferences from label warnings, marked partial, and the unit's protocol governs practice.
jurisdiction_note: US FDA label only. EMA, MHRA and SFDA labels were not read; indications, warnings and presentations differ by country and by manufacturer.

items.text: The label describes cefazolin in dextrose injection as a cephalosporin antibacterial indicated for treatment of infections caused by susceptible isolates in adult and paediatric patients.
Ask about penicillin and other beta-lactam allergy before the first dose and report the history.
Monitoring frequency and alarm limits follow the unit's protocol for this medicine.

The label warns seizures may occur, particularly in patients with renal impairment whose dosage is not reduced appropriately, so unexplained seizure activity should prompt review of renal function and dosing; it also notes cefazolin may be associated with a fall in prothrombin activity, so prothrombin time should be monitored in at-risk patients, and lists Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea among its warnings.

The registered cefazolin label warns of seizures in renal impairment when treatment is not appropriately adjusted. Review renal function and clarify the prescription with pharmacy or the treating team when renal function worsens. Obtain the details of any previous beta-lactam reaction rather than recording only an unspecified allergy.

The Baxter label identifies renal or hepatic impairment, poor nutrition, prolonged antimicrobial use and previous anticoagulant therapy as risk factors for reduced prothrombin activity. Review ordered coagulation testing in at-risk patients.

Probenecid can inhibit renal elimination of cefazolin; the registered premixed dextrose product advises against concurrent use. Review the actual product and medication list with pharmacy or the responsible clinician.
Cross-hypersensitivity may occur in a proportion of patients with a history of penicillin allergy; if an allergic reaction occurs the drug is discontinued (prescriber decision).
Serious and occasionally fatal hypersensitivity (anaphylactic) reactions have been reported with cephalosporins, penicillins and other beta-lactams.
Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea may range from mild diarrhoea to fatal colitis and should be evaluated if diarrhoea occurs.
Cefazolin may be associated with a fall in prothrombin activity; prothrombin time should be monitored in patients at risk.
The label lists hypersensitivity reactions among the serious adverse reactions described.

Stop and summon emergency help for serious allergy or seizures; urgently notify the treating team for new neurological change, severe diarrhoea, or unexpected bleeding. Follow authorised cessation and supportive-care procedures.

Use the unit's early warning score (for example, the Royal College of Physicians' NEWS2 track-and-trigger system) to standardise recognition of acute deterioration: a medium aggregate score is a key trigger for an urgent clinical review, and a high aggregate score triggers an emergency clinical response. This is a generic nursing escalation framework, not specific to this medicine; it does not replace this medicine's own escalation triggers, which remain local protocol.
Record the product and order checks, monitoring results, adverse events and escalation per unit standard.
Institution-specific preparation: follow your pharmacy's preparation standard and the product labelling. This library gives no preparation or concentration instructions.
Institution-specific dosing: follow the prescriber's order and your institution's approved protocol. This library gives no dosing instructions.

monitoring.text: Check penicillin and beta-lactam allergy history.
Watch for rash, breathing difficulty and swelling.
Review prothrombin time in patients at risk.
Report allergic signs, persistent diarrhoea or bleeding.
Review renal function, prior allergy reaction details and new seizure activity; report worsening renal function for prescription review before further administration where clinically appropriate.
Check for renal or hepatic impairment, poor nutritional status, prolonged therapy or anticoagulant use; review ordered prothrombin time and report new bleeding.
Flag concurrent probenecid and worsening renal function; clarify the prescription with pharmacy.
